what_its_for: This medicine is an antibiotic used to fight certain bacterial infections, including pneumonia (lung infection), skin infections, and infections in your belly area (abdomen). It works by stopping bacteria from growing and multiplying. It does NOT work for viral infections like the common cold or flu.
how_to_take: This medicine is given directly into your vein (intravenously, or 'IV') by a nurse or healthcare provider in a hospital or clinic setting. It is slowly dripped into your vein over about 60 minutes (1 hour). Never try to give yourself this medicine at home unless your doctor or nurse has specifically trained you and told you it is safe to do so. Make sure the IV bag is clear and free of particles before use — do not use it if the liquid looks cloudy or has floating pieces in it.
dosing: The usual adult dose is 400 mg (one 250 mL IV bag) given once every 24 hours (once daily). Your doctor will decide exactly how long your treatment should last, which is typically 5 to 21 days depending on the type of infection. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions — do not stop treatment early even if you start feeling better, as this can allow the infection to come back.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given by a healthcare professional in a clinical setting, it is unlikely that you will miss a dose. However, if for any reason a scheduled infusion is missed or delayed, contact your doctor or nurse right away so they can reschedule it as soon as possible. Do not try to 'double up' or take two doses at once to make up for a missed one.
storage: This medicine should be stored at room temperature between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Do not refrigerate or freeze the IV bag. Keep it away from direct light. Do not use the bag after the expiration date printed on the label. Once opened or mixed, follow your pharmacist's or nurse's specific instructions on how long it can safely be used.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking antacids, vitamins, or supplements that contain aluminum, magnesium, calcium, iron, or zinc within a few hours of your moxifloxacin treatment, as these can reduce how well the medicine works. Avoid spending too much time in the sun or using tanning beds, as this medicine can make your skin more sensitive to sunlight — use sunscreen and wear protective clothing when outdoors. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery if you feel dizzy, confused, or lightheaded. Limit or avoid alcohol during treatment. Tell your doctor about ALL other medicines you take, especially heart rhythm medicines, antidepressants, or antipsychotics, as dangerous interactions are possible.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor immediately or go to the emergency room if you experience any of the following: a fast, pounding, or irregular heartbeat or chest pain (this could be a serious heart rhythm problem); sudden tendon pain, swelling, or a 'snapping' feeling — especially in your heel, shoulder, or hand (this could mean a tendon rupture); numbness, tingling, weakness, or burning pain in your arms or legs (nerve damage); severe diarrhea that is watery or bloody (this could be a dangerous bowel infection); serious skin rash, blistering, or peeling; confusion, hallucinations, seizures, or thoughts of harming yourself; signs of an allergic reaction such as hives, difficulty breathing, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat; yellowing of your skin or eyes, or dark urine (signs of liver problems). Also contact your doctor if your infection does not seem to be getting better after a few days of treatment.
when_it_works: Many patients start to feel better within 2 to 3 days of starting treatment. However, it is very important to complete your full course of treatment even if you feel well sooner. Stopping early can allow bacteria to survive and your infection to return, possibly making it harder to treat next time.
special_populations: Older adults (65 years and older): You may have a higher risk of tendon problems and heart rhythm changes. Report any unusual pain, swelling, or heartbeat changes to your doctor right away. Patients with liver problems: Use caution — your doctor will monitor you closely, as this medicine may affect the liver. Patients with heart conditions: Tell your doctor if you have ever had a heart rhythm problem called 'QT prolongation' or if you take any heart medicines, as moxifloxacin can affect your heart rhythm. Pregnant or breastfeeding patients: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding — this medicine should generally be avoided in pregnancy, and it may pass into breast milk. Children and teenagers: The safety of this medicine in patients under 18 years of age has not been fully established. It is typically only used in children when no safer option is available. Patients with a history of myasthenia gravis (a muscle weakness disorder): This medicine can make your symptoms much worse — tell your doctor right away if this applies to you.
